sections.s06.s0: Work in order: returns and money handling first (s0.0 to s0.2), then bias, risk and portfolio maths (s0.3 to s0.6), then data storage and code discipline (s0.7, s0.8). Spend about two thirds of the time running small pandas experiments on real daily prices and one third reading. This is education only, not investment advice.
sections.s06.s1: Build in the listed order: the simulation with costs, the lookahead test, the metrics, the benchmark, then walk-forward. Keep each part in its own module with tests. Treat the whole build as a data-analysis exercise, not a trading system.

s06.s0.0.how: Load daily prices for one stock and compute simple returns with pct_change() and log returns with np.log(p).diff(). Check that log returns sum to the total log return and simple returns compound with (1 + r).prod(). Compare close and adjusted close across a known split date.
s06.s0.0.done: You can say which return type adds across time and which across assets, and your split day shows no fake -50% return.

s06.s0.1.how: Check sum([0.1] * 10) == 1.0 with floats, then with Decimal('0.1'). Write a fee function that takes Decimal amounts and rounds with quantize(Decimal('0.01'), rounding=ROUND_HALF_EVEN). Note where float is fine: returns, volatility and other statistics.
s06.s0.1.done: You can explain why Decimal(0.1) differs from Decimal('0.1') and when a float result is acceptable.

s06.s0.2.how: Load two markets with different closing times, set each index's zone with tz_localize, convert both to UTC with tz_convert, then resample('W').last() and join. Use merge_asof to attach the latest known value of one series to the other without looking ahead.
s06.s0.2.done: Your joined frame has no row where one market's value comes from a later timestamp than the row's own time.

s06.s0.3.how: Reproduce each bias on purpose: shift a signal the wrong way to create lookahead, backtest only today's index members to see survivorship, and rerun with 10 basis points of fees and slippage per trade. Write down how much each one changes the result.
s06.s0.3.done: You can name the bias behind a too-good backtest and show the one-line fix for lookahead.

s06.s0.4.how: From daily returns compute annualised volatility with std() * sqrt(252), the Sharpe ratio as mean excess return over its standard deviation (annualised), maximum drawdown from cummax() of the equity curve, and 95% historical VaR with quantile(0.05).
s06.s0.4.done: Your four functions match hand-calculated values on a 10-day example to 6 decimal places.

s06.s0.5.how: Take 5 to 10 assets, estimate expected returns and a covariance matrix, and use PyPortfolioOpt's EfficientFrontier to get minimum-volatility and maximum-Sharpe weights. Compare them with equal weights, then nudge one expected return and watch how far the weights move.
s06.s0.5.done: You can explain why optimised weights swing when expected returns change slightly, and why equal weights are a fair baseline.

s06.s0.6.how: Build features from past prices and score a model with TimeSeriesSplit, then with KFold(shuffle=True). Then write a walk-forward loop by hand: fit on a window, test on the next block, move both forward.
s06.s0.6.done: You can show that the shuffled split scores higher and explain which future information leaked into it.

s06.s0.7.how: Pick one free data API and read its rate limits. Write a downloader that sets timeouts, retries with backoff, caches raw responses and saves cleaned data with to_parquet. Store the source, download date and price adjustments in a metadata file next to the data.
s06.s0.7.done: Your research script reads only local files and gives the same numbers with the network switched off.

s06.s0.8.how: List what research code can skip and execution code cannot: input validation, logging, error handling, safe restarts and reconciliation of records. Take one of your notebooks and mark every place that would fail silently if it ran unattended.
s06.s0.8.done: You can list five differences between research and execution code and point to an example of each in your own code.

s06.s1.0.how: Load daily prices, compute a moving-average crossover with rolling(), turn it into positions and earn the next day's return. Charge fees and slippage in basis points on every change in position, and keep the cost settings in one config object.
s06.s1.0.done: With costs set to zero you get the gross result, and raising costs lowers returns by trades times cost per trade.

s06.s1.1.how: Route every strategy through one function that shifts signals by one bar before they meet returns. Write a pytest test that changes prices after day t and asserts that positions up to day t stay the same.
s06.s1.1.done: The test fails when you remove the shift and passes when it is in place.

s06.s1.2.how: Write one report() function that takes a daily return series and returns total and annualised return, annualised volatility, Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown. Reuse the risk functions you already checked by hand instead of writing new ones.
s06.s1.2.done: report() reproduces your hand-checked example and runs unchanged on any daily return series.

s06.s1.3.how: Run buy-and-hold on the same asset, dates and cost settings. Plot both equity curves from (1 + r).cumprod() and put both reports side by side, adding the strategy's time in the market so a drawdown saved by sitting in cash is visible.
s06.s1.3.done: Strategy and benchmark cover identical dates, and you can say whether the strategy beat buy-and-hold after costs.

s06.s1.4.how: Split the history into consecutive train and test windows, choose parameters on each train window only, and record results on the test window that follows. Join the test windows into one out-of-sample equity curve and report it apart from in-sample figures.
s06.s1.4.done: The report has separate in-sample and out-of-sample tables, and no test date falls inside its own training window.
